figures.caption: Table 2: Family-by-family patching results across the four main late-route variants on the 293- pair cohort. Each route cell reports mean ∆ / flip rate, where a more negative mean ∆ indicates a stronger weakening of the malicious judgment under the intervention and therefore stronger dependence on the intervened route. Route abbreviations are: Minimal = L0H11 → L12H15/L12H5/L12H4, Top-5 = L12H15/L12H5/L12H4/L12H2/L12H28, H2-free = L12H15/L12H5/L12H4/L12H28, and H28-free = L12H15/L12H5/L12H4/L12H2.

Figure 2: Indicator-transformation evasion flowchart for the strongest current failure modes. The attack preserves malicious behavior while replacing or reconstructing a canonical indicator; the inherited malicious-evidence signal remains internally available, but fine-tuned feed-forward computation near the classification boundary reverses or misuses that signal before final classification.

Figure 1: Cross-model circuit summary. Foundation-Sec and Llama share the broad PowerShell classification skeleton, including the early detector and late integration layer, but fine-tuning shifts which late heads dominate and adds indicator-token semantics to the final classification signal.

Table 6: Representative side-by-side examples of successful evasion from both benchmark tiers. In direct_v1, replacing the explicit Invoke-WebRequest token with the alias iwr is sufficient to flip Foundation-Sec’s prediction. In reconstructive_v2, a format-string reconstruction of Invoke-Expression likewise produces a Foundation-Sec miss while preserving the surrounding payload logic.

Figure 5: Mean logit-diff delta when indicator tokens are mean-ablated, broken down by indicator family and model. A negative delta means removing the indicator tokens reduces malicious confidence (the token was acting as a driver of the malicious prediction). A positive delta means removing them increases malicious confidence (the token was acting as a suppressor). Invoke-WebRequest shows the clearest divergence: Foundation-Sec (orange) has a large positive delta (+1.13), while Llama (blue) shows a strong negative delta (−1.60). This divergence identifies Invoke-WebRequest as the family where the canonical indicator changed role between models and where alias substitution (iwr) produces consistent classification failures. The DownloadFile Llama bar extends below the axis limit (value: −8.0); the y-axis is capped at −5.5 to keep the smaller-delta families readable.

Figure 4: Scatter plots of predicted versus actual Layer-12 head contributions for each of the four core heads (L12H4, L12H5, L12H15, L12H28). Each point is one malicious script; the dashed diagonal is the identity line. Colors indicate indicator family. The tight alignment around the diagonal across all four panels confirms that the probe’s r = 0.80–0.87 performance is consistent and not driven by outliers or a single family.
Table 3: Cross-model circuit comparison. Llama uses the same early detector and late writer layer as Foundation-Sec, but its strongest route is more diffuse and shifts late dominance toward L12H28.

Figure 3: Cross-validated linear probe performance (Ridge regression, 5-fold CV). Blue bars show how well Llama’s resid_pre13 activation predicts each Layer-12 head’s contribution to the contrastive direction (r = 0.80–0.87, n = 206). Orange bars show cross-model transfer: the same Llama activations predicting Foundation-Sec’s circuit dependence under top-5 ablation (r = 0.41) and indicator-token L2 sensitivity (r = 0.83). The high within-model r values confirm each head’s contribution is linearly encoded at the circuit boundary; the lower ablation-delta transfer (r = 0.41) reflects the ceiling imposed by the cross-model fine-tuning gap.
Table 4: Foundation-Sec evasion benchmark status. Variants satisfy the parse or manual-validation checks and behavioral invariants from the implemented pipeline.

Table 1: Reusable evasion benchmark structure. The direct_v1 tier applies direct syntax-preserving rewrites to visible command, token, and method forms, reconstructive_v2 uses composed expressions that reconstruct suspicious commands or strings at runtime, and case_mutation_v3 changes token casing while preserving syntax and arguments. Variants are accepted only after parse or manual-validation checks and invariant checks for valid PowerShell syntax and preserved behavior.
